title: Inside America’s Economic Divide- AI, Tariffs, & The Fed - The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 29

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Inside America’s Economic Divide- AI, Tariffs, & The Fed - The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 29.docx

speakers: Steve Leeman (caption spelling; CNBC senior economics reporter)
summary: Eisman interviews a CNBC economics reporter on a K-shaped US economy: AI capex vs weak ex-AI economy, tariffs, consumer, Fed politics and the GFC. Approach is macro narrative and pattern recognition. Main conclusions: AI boom is real but returns are unproven, tariff damage is early and masked by AI.

coverage.note: Intro and teaser; GDP vs AI capex math; market vs economy
AI capex reflexivity; ex-AI economy; tariffs and margins; small business; CarMax
Consumer: car loans, cruise lines, credit; student loans
Youth unemployment; AI and coders; users vs providers of technology
Dot-com analogy; AI capex funding; valuation; tariffs start
Liberation Day reversal; funding stress; tariff hit industries
Tariff effects on firms; effective vs statutory rate; start of Fed talk
Fed and political pressure; Volcker; long-end resistance
Fed chairs and communication; QE criticism
Greenspan critique; underwriting; subprime pattern; CDO growth
Russia in the 1990s: inflation and institutions

completeness_estimate: 0.92 - first reader caught nearly every idea (only a data-gap caveat, stacked metal tariffs, tariff evasion, the Kaplan disagreement and Bernanke deflation tools missed) but misattributed about ten claims between the two Steves

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: If you take all the money that Meta, Google, Amazon, right, Oracle, etc., etc., are spending on AI, it's over 400 billion.
claims.claim: Hyperscaler AI capex (over $400B) is nearly as large as expected US GDP growth ($530B at 1.8% on $29.18T), so the economy excluding AI spending is roughly flat.
claims.indicator: hyperscaler AI capex vs nominal GDP growth
claims.conditions: Depends on the 1.8% consensus growth figure and on how much capex is imported rather than domestic output
claims.testable: partly - capex and GDP are public, but the domestic-content adjustment is not stated

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: there's a pie and we're going to basically dole out pieces of that pie and uh how much of the pie goes to the corporations, how much goes to people.
claims.claim: Long-run market and economy analysis should be framed as how the GDP pie is split between corporations and people, not by technical charts and momentum; the market and the economy are different things.
claims.indicator: corporate profit share of GDP vs labour share
claims.testable: partly - profit share and labour share are measurable but no rule is given

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: he said the momentum will continue as long as the momentum continues.
claims.claim: The market is in a speculative fervor in which momentum is self-reinforcing (quote attributed to Josh Brown).
claims.conditions: Holds until the market stops rewarding the behaviour

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: as long as the market is rewarding companies for increasing their investment in AI, AI investment will continue.
claims.claim: Corporate AI capex is reflexive: it keeps rising while share prices reward each increase, so spending persists until the market's reward stops.
claims.indicator: AI capex announcements vs share price reaction
claims.conditions: Ends when investors demand returns instead of more investment
claims.testable: partly - could test price reaction to capex guidance

correction.issue: wrong speaker: Leeman says this, explaining Josh Brown's momentum remark
correction.fix: Steve Leeman: corporate AI capex is reflexive; it continues as long as the market rewards companies for raising AI investment.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: companies would continue to fire people and not hire as long as the announcements of firings was greeted by company share prices rising.
claims.claim: After 2000 firms kept cutting jobs and not hiring while layoff announcements were rewarded with higher share prices, so market reward drives corporate labour decisions.
claims.conditions: Needs the market to reward layoffs
claims.testable: partly - event study of layoff announcements

correction.issue: wrong speaker: Leeman recalls the post-2000 layoff pattern
correction.fix: Steve Leeman: after 2000 firms kept firing and not hiring as long as layoff announcements lifted their share prices, so market reward drives corporate decisions.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: if you look at investment X AI not much going on you look at the other things
claims.claim: Investment excluding AI is flat to down, because of tariffs, so the strength in aggregate investment and equities is concentrated in AI.
claims.conditions: Little visibility because of the government shutdown and missing data
claims.testable: partly - non-AI capex is measurable but the data was delayed

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: So they're sucking up tariffs in margin and how long that continues is what's unclear to me.
claims.claim: Companies with high starting margins are absorbing tariff costs in margins; how long they can do this determines when tariffs reach prices, profits and jobs.
claims.indicator: corporate profit margins vs tariff cost
claims.conditions: Works while margins start high
claims.testable: partly - margin data by tariff exposure

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: a large company has departments that do this.
claims.claim: Small businesses lack the staff to find alternative suppliers, check tariff rates or obtain exemptions, so tariffs hit the engine of growth harder than large firms.
claims.testable: partly - small-business surveys vs large-cap results

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: there's a K that goes up and a K that goes down and there's a big piece of the K. It's flat flat.
claims.claim: The K-shaped economy has an upward leg, a downward leg and a large flat middle, so the shape is not simply a split between winners and losers.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: used cars is kind of a a nice sort of what I call a canary in the coal mine kind of view into what's happening in the consumer.
claims.claim: Used-car lenders and sellers are an early indicator of consumer stress.
claims.indicator: used-car retailer results and loan loss provisions
claims.testable: yes - auto delinquency and provisions are public

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: CarMax missed badly. They took a loan loss provision that was significantly higher than people expected.
claims.claim: CarMax missed and raised its loan loss provision, and buyers shifted to older cars they can afford, which Eisman reads as evidence of a stressed lower-income consumer.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: there's a thesis out there. I don't know yet how much I subscribe to it that the consumer is I don't know if the word is tapped out
claims.claim: The thesis that the consumer is tapped out and no longer increasing spending is considered but not adopted.
claims.testable: partly - retail sales and real spending

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: when all the bills come due and you can't pay one, the first thing you pay is your car loan, right? It's to get to work.
claims.claim: Car loans are the last obligation a stressed household stops paying, so rising auto delinquencies mean broad household stress.

correction.issue: wrong speaker: Leeman explains why the car loan is the last bill paid
correction.fix: Steve Leeman: households pay the car loan first because they need the car to get to work, so rising auto delinquencies signal serious household stress.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: the cost of parts are going up for two reasons.
claims.claim: Tariffs and more repair demand from owners keeping old cars are both raising car parts costs, which worsens the burden on stretched drivers.

correction.issue: wrong speaker: Leeman makes the car-parts point
correction.fix: Steve Leeman: car parts costs are rising both from tariffs and from owners repairing older cars to keep them running.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: Carnival just said they're like sold out through 26 and the bookings for 27 are better than they've ever seen two years ahead.
claims.claim: Cruise demand is strong with sold-out bookings, which counters the tapped-out-consumer thesis; Liesman says bookings are middle income with jobs.
claims.conditions: Applies to middle-income consumers with jobs

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: The cruise companies never really raised price for the last several years and now they're only just catching up a little bit.
claims.claim: Cruise lines kept prices flat while hotel prices rose multiples after COVID, so cruises are cheap relative to hotels and have pricing power left.
claims.direction: cruise lines profit from catch-up pricing

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: It doesn't look like 2008 or 2007, anywhere near that.
claims.claim: Outside car loans, consumer credit looks healthy (debt levels not overstretched), so the consumer has capacity to borrow; modest rate cuts would help.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: the extent to which the student loan repayments may be stressing the car data
claims.claim: Resumed student loan repayments may be pushing car delinquencies higher, so part of the auto stress is not a general credit signal.
claims.indicator: student loan payments vs auto delinquencies

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: the current unemployment rate in the United States is four and a half percent. Youth unemployment's around 11.
claims.claim: Youth unemployment (around 11%) is far above the headline rate (4.5%), and recent computer science graduates report difficulty finding jobs.
claims.conditions: Anecdotes about programmers are unverified

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: AI is is programming like there's no tomorrow.
claims.claim: AI is replacing entry-level and even experienced coding work, so careers once recommended for retraining no longer absorb workers.
claims.testable: partly - hiring data in software roles

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: instead of the the engine being off the airplane for 6 months, it was off the airplane for like 6 weeks.
claims.claim: Computerised machine tools once cut a turbine repair from 6 months to 6 weeks, an example of general-purpose technology producing a generational productivity gain; AI could do the same.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: I am always interested not in the providers of the technology but the users of the technology because if the users if the profit does not acrue to the users of technology then you're going to hit a dead end.
claims.claim: The AI boom only pays off if profits accrue to the users of the technology, not just its suppliers; he wants the market to pay multiples on users before being convinced.
claims.indicator: profit growth at AI adopters vs AI suppliers

correction.issue: wrong speaker: the users-vs-providers view comes from Leeman (who built a PC, edited over CompuServe from Florida), not Eisman
correction.fix: Steve Leeman: the AI boom pays off only if profits accrue to the users of the technology; he will be convinced when the market pays multiples on users, not on the investment.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: we're going to be spending trillions on this but because it will reap tension because of tens of trillions of returns.
claims.claim: Nvidia's argument is that trillions in AI spend will return tens of trillions.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: He was 1,000% correct on both predictions, but it wasn't a straight line.
claims.claim: In the dot-com era the technology thesis was right but the path was not a straight line, because early returns were absent and capex eventually stopped.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: they're spending it out of cash flow. So that in itself is much healthier
claims.claim: This AI capex cycle is funded from cash flow, so if it fails the loss is an equity loss, not a leverage loss or systemic risk.
claims.indicator: funding of AI capex from cash flow vs debt
claims.conditions: Changes if capex funding moves to debt

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: the AI Google search, I'll be the first to admit, is better than the old Google search, but it's not a thousand times better.
claims.claim: AI returns have not yet appeared: the product is better but not by a multiple that justifies the spending, so the payoff is still awaited.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: Does the market make up wake up one morning Steve and say you know what I don't want to see more investment.
claims.claim: The regime changes when the market stops rewarding more AI investment and demands returns, which Eisman says is certainly coming though the timing is unknown.
claims.indicator: market reaction to AI capex vs revenue evidence
claims.conditions: Trigger is a shift from investment to return focus

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: picking the winners at the right price.
claims.claim: In technology booms the hard part is picking winners at the right price; even winners such as Nvidia can be bought at a price that destroys returns.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: that in good time in good times, right? People care about stories and in bad times they care about balance sheets.
claims.claim: In good times investors value stories and ignore valuation; in bad times they focus on balance sheets.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: Any stock. Sell me some stock.
claims.claim: A drunk man banging on a broker's door at 3 a.m. during the 1993 Russian boom illustrates the late-stage speculative-mania anecdote.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: the tariff levels that are currently being imposed in most cases are lower than the worst case scenario.
claims.claim: Implemented tariff levels are below the Liberation Day worst case but far above pre-2025 levels.

correction.issue: wrong speaker: Eisman sets up the tariff question (levels below Liberation Day worst case but far above before)
correction.fix: Steve Eisman: implemented tariffs are below the Liberation Day worst case but far above pre-2025 levels, yet have had little visible economic impact so far.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: A lot of the Armageddon apocalyptic forecasts were from that period of time.
claims.claim: Apocalyptic economic forecasts were tied to the April 2-9 tariff levels that were later cut, so economists were not wrong on their inputs but misjudged the president's willingness to back off.
claims.conditions: Forecasts need a political judgement about policy reversal

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: On the way back up on the plane, the president decided to drastically amend the tariffs.
claims.claim: Tariff policy was reversed after a bank warning of a meltdown, i.e. financial market stress limits how far policy goes.
claims.conditions: Policy backs off when markets or funding break

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: the iners of the market were fairly close to seizing up at that time.
claims.claim: Contacts in repo and Fed funds trading said they were not the story yet, showing funding markets were close to seizing in April 2025; calling market insiders is a gauge of plumbing stress.
claims.indicator: repo and Fed funds market functioning
claims.testable: partly - funding spreads can be tested, anecdote is not

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: plenty of industries that have been hit by these tariffs and their um their stocks have fallen tremendously and it's been papered over by what's happening in AI
claims.claim: Tariff-hit industries have fallen sharply but index-level results are masked by AI stocks, producing a K-shaped market.
claims.testable: yes - sector returns vs tariff exposure

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: they're going to lay off 8% 10% of their workforce. So that's still to come.
claims.claim: Tariff-driven closures and layoffs (Orvis example) lag the policy, so the labour damage is still to come.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: One of the things we have which is not present in Europe and other places in the world are the ability to change business's ability to change and pivot.
claims.claim: The dynamism of US businesses to re-source and pivot cushions tariff shocks.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: Does the business model even stand anymore when you're paying 15%.
claims.claim: A small business earning $200k may not survive 15% tariffs on its inputs.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: which is don't put tariffs on inputs. That's what we did.
claims.claim: Tariffs on inputs hurt manufacturers that add value domestically, contradicting economists' advice.
claims.conditions: Unless they can re-source or avoid the tariff

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: one of the great um fudge factors in all trade is intercomp pricing.
claims.claim: Firms lower tariff bills by shifting cost attribution to the domestic entity through intercompany pricing, so the effective tariff rate falls over time.

correction.issue: wrong speaker: Leeman continues on intercompany pricing as a tariff fudge factor
correction.fix: Steve Leeman: firms lower tariff bills by shifting cost attribution to the domestic entity through intercompany pricing, so the average effective tariff falls over time.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: The last data I saw showed the effective tariff on goods being imported is 10%. They believe the actual tariff rate is 18%.
claims.claim: Effective tariff is 10% against a stated 18%, so only half is seen; if companies hold exposure at 10% the economy is okay.
claims.conditions: Holds if avoidance limits exposure

correction.issue: wrong speaker: Leeman, backing up his 'it's early' point
correction.fix: Steve Leeman: the effective tariff on imports is 10% against an estimated actual rate of 18%, so only half has been seen; but companies may cap exposure at 10%, in which case the economy is okay.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: the Federal Reserve does not exist in a political vacuum.
claims.claim: The Fed operates within a political climate: it hiked 75bp in 2022 with political permission to fight inflation, because neither party pushed back.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: it's not entirely clear to me that in the absence of the pressure the president has put on the Fed that they would have cut at the last meeting.
claims.claim: Presidential pressure made a cut politically easy, and the Fed is a little tight now, so a cut may reflect pressure as much as data.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: I don't think Vulker would be cutting here.
claims.claim: Volcker would not have cut with inflation at 3% against a 2% target and rising.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: and no resistance right now to 25. At some point it'll be interesting to see especially if the long end provides some resistance if they go beyond another 25 or 50 from here.
claims.claim: The Fed follows the path of least resistance, and the long end of the yield curve is where resistance to more cuts would appear.
claims.indicator: long-end yields as response to Fed cuts
claims.direction: long yields rise if cuts go beyond 25 to 50bp
claims.conditions: Applies if cuts go beyond another 25 to 50bp

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: He instituted the press conference. He instituted um the uh SCP, the forecast, um the dots
claims.claim: Bernanke made the Fed more transparent (press conferences, forecasts, dots), which Powell extended to every meeting, so policy is now guided by communication.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: the Fed's uh, use of unconventional monetary policy tools led to vast inequality helping asset holders rather than people who were working.
claims.claim: The Treasury Secretary criticised QE as raising asset prices and inequality; Liesman and Eisman accept it raised asset prices but say the alternative was worse.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: it's a 30,000word critique of the Fed by the Treasury Secretary, which was unprecedented
claims.claim: The Treasury Secretary's long public critique of the Fed signals unusual political pressure on Fed independence.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: I don't think the Fed is the first font of it I think there are other reasons um especially the returns to technology
claims.claim: Inequality is driven mainly by returns to technology, not by the Fed.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: the banks became way too levered. a big asset class, subprime, blew up and banks that were systemically important owned the asset class.
claims.claim: The financial crisis came from excessive bank leverage, a blown-up asset class (subprime) and systemically important banks owning it.
claims.indicator: bank leverage and exposure to a single asset class

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: He allowed all the leverage to take place because, as he's admitted, he trusted them.
claims.claim: Regulators who trust banks allow leverage to build and ignore fraud warnings, as Greenspan did in 2005 and 2006.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: there should be a derivative for every risk.
claims.claim: The economic consensus that a derivative should exist for every risk led regulators and economists to welcome derivative growth in the early 2000s.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: you could generate all of these graphs showing endless returns into the future that nobody had ever seen before.
claims.claim: Cheap modelling tools (Lotus and Excel) enabled endless-return projections that fuelled the 1980s Florida real estate boom, as computing power later let anyone price any derivative.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: he was too regular with his rate increases.
claims.claim: Greenspan's predictable quarterly hikes let the Street game the system; less clarity might have been better.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: I thought, as you said, they were going to take care of themselves, and they didn't.
claims.claim: Greenspan admitted he was wrong that derivative markets would self-regulate.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: We got done lending lending to everybody who was creditworthy and we still had money left over.
claims.claim: Late in a credit boom lenders exhaust creditworthy borrowers and then lend to the rest (2006 mortgage standards were 'can you breathe'), which sets up the bust.
claims.testable: yes - underwriting standard surveys and loan performance

correction.issue: partly misattributed: the 'done lending to everybody creditworthy' line is a Deutsche Bank derivatives head quoted by Leeman; Eisman adds the 2006 'can you breathe' underwriting line
correction.fix: Steve Leeman (quoting a Deutsche Bank derivatives head) with Eisman agreeing: late in the credit boom lenders had lent to every creditworthy borrower and still had money left, so standards collapsed (2006 underwriting was 'can you breathe').

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: the people who were running them were the same guys who were running them in '98. They just changed the names.
claims.claim: Subprime lenders failed in 1998 and the same people re-emerged in 2002, so recurring cycles are driven by the same operators; spotting repeat players gave an early warning.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: we're growing at $40 billion a year
claims.claim: CLO and CDO issuance growth ($40 billion then $100 billion per year) was the clue that the structured credit boom was becoming systemic.

correction.issue: wrong speaker: the CLO/CDO chess-tournament story ($40B then $100B a year) is Leeman's
correction.fix: Steve Leeman: CLO and CDO issuance growing at $40B and then $100B a year was the clue that structured credit was becoming big enough to be systemic.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: Meil Lynch had a 20 something% stake in it. And they decided it was better to let it go down prop it up.
claims.claim: A sponsor's decision to let a subprime originator fail rather than prop it up signalled the beginning of the failures.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: turns into inflation the next month.
claims.claim: In Russia in the 1990s a budget deficit turned into inflation within a month, showing fiscal deficits monetised quickly into prices.
claims.conditions: Applies where deficits are monetised

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: A c country is going to develop a legal code that it's its own on its own
claims.claim: Institutions such as legal codes cannot be imported; foreign-written codes and myths fail, one reason Russian reform failed.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: the Russian government would not accept that $1 billion in unemployment insurance because because of the way it appeared
claims.claim: Reforms that look humiliating (Russia refusing a $1B unemployment fund) foster the backlash that opposed them.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: within two years of privatizing the oil companies the oil companies turned around a 20-year decline in oil output from the Soviet Union.
claims.claim: Privatising Russian oil companies reversed a 20-year decline in output within two years because of ownership incentives.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: We're going to allow the price to float and that will move the oil.
claims.claim: Officials who had never lived with market prices could not grasp that letting prices float would move oil to a region, illustrating price-signal allocation.

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: I'm also concerned and I we don't have any data at all because of the shutdown. But we even if the shutdown weren't happening, we wouldn't have data.
claims.claim: The tariff hit to small businesses cannot be measured: the government shutdown halted official data, and even normal releases do not capture it, so the weak leg of the economy is largely invisible in the data.
claims.indicator: official small business / tariff impact data (missing during shutdown)
claims.conditions: government shutdown; small firms poorly covered by official data

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: these uh guys who import the fishing reels made in China and Japan were going to get hit two ways. One was on the import tariff and then on the content of the metal.
claims.claim: Importers of goods containing metal pay twice, the country tariff plus the tariff on metal content, so the effective burden on such products is higher than the headline country rate.
claims.indicator: country tariff plus metal-content tariff on imported goods
claims.conditions: stacked country and sectoral (metal) tariffs
claims.testable: partly - margins of importers of metal-content goods vs others

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: There were huge tariffs on the import of computer equipment. So, we paid a guy to do the importing from us. So, they arrived in boxes labeled children's clothes and that was exempt.
claims.claim: High tariffs create evasion (mislabelling, paid intermediaries), as with computer imports into 1990s Russia, and companies are already finding ways around current US tariffs, so collected rates fall below statutory rates.
claims.conditions: high tariffs with exemptions that can be exploited
claims.testable: partly - customs revenue vs statutory rate over time

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: would any of the political pressure that the president is trying to impose on the Fed be discussed at a Fed meeting? And he he was like adamant about it. He said absolutely not.
claims.claim: Former Dallas Fed president Rob Kaplan insists political pressure is never discussed at FOMC meetings; Leeman disagrees in substance, saying the pressure plays in the room without being discussed and the Fed both creates and reacts to the political milieu.
claims.conditions: disagreement: insider (Kaplan) vs reporter (Leeman) view

claims.speaker: Steve Leeman
claims.quote: I did an interview with him in 2002 about the helicopter. The money was dropped from a helicopter that the Fed had all of these avenues and abilities to fight deflation.
claims.claim: Bernanke arrived having already worked out (2002 helicopter-money speech) that the Fed has many tools to fight deflation even at zero rates, which made him suited to launch QE in the financial crisis.
claims.conditions: deflation risk at the zero bound
